interest: Shows 1930s winding-down of foreign perpetual leaseholds in Japan, and American land ownership and alien land-law disputes.
overview: State Department decimal file 894.5211 covers the period from October 1931 to October 1939 and documents legal, diplomatic, and practical questions surrounding the rights of United States nationals to hold, acquire, inherit, and lease real property in Japan, as well as reciprocal restrictions under U.S. state alien land laws. Major subjects include British diplomatic initiatives in 1931 to terminate perpetual leaseholdings held by foreigners in Japanese treaty ports in exchange for government bonds and fee simple title; legal inquiries from American executors and attorneys regarding probate procedures, succession duties, and the devise of real estate in Japan (such as missionary properties in Karuizawa and estates in Yokohama and Nara); State Department analyses of the Japanese Civil Code, the Japanese Alien Land Law of 1925, and bilateral treaties of commerce and navigation (1894 and 1911); lists of American citizens known to own land in fee simple in Japan; state-level alien land law inquiries from Georgia, Idaho, and Washington concerning whether treaties granted reciprocal ownership or leasing rights to Japanese subjects; and union protests in Hawaii against commercial land acquisitions by Japanese enterprises.

subfiles.about: Cross-references Despatch No. 348 regarding negotiations to wind up foreign perpetual leaseholds in Japan.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville (Chargé d'Affaires a.i., Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Neville reports on American cooperation with British leaseholders to liquidate perpetual leases in Japan.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Tokyo Despatch No. 348 on Perpetual Leases

subfiles.about: Reports on British diplomatic initiatives to terminate perpetual leases held by foreigners in Japan and requests Department instructions.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville (Chargé d'Affaires a.i., Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Neville reports British leaseholders are negotiating to convert perpetual leases to fee simple with equal taxation; American leaseholders seek to join, and he asks Washington for instructions.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 348 from Edwin L. Neville on Liquidation of Foreign Perpetual Leaseholds

subfiles.about: Inquires regarding Japanese legal requirements for effectuating the devise of real property in Karuizawa under an American will.
subfiles.from: Isaac A. Pennypacker (Pepper, Bodine, Stokes & Schoch, Philadelphia)
subfiles.summary: Pennypacker asks State how to effect a will's devise of Karuizawa real estate inherited from missionary Correll, under Japanese law.
subfiles.title: Letter from Isaac A. Pennypacker on Devise of Karuizawa Real Estate Under Correll Will

subfiles.about: Declines to express an official opinion on foreign law and refers the inquirer to private law firms specializing in Japanese law.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck (Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, for the Acting Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck declines to opine on Japanese real estate law, directing Pennypacker to New York attorneys while disclaiming responsibility for them.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Isaac A. Pennypacker Regarding Japanese Real Estate Law

subfiles.about: Apologizes to Isaac A. Pennypacker for the delay in answering his inquiry caused by a misplaced departmental file.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck apologizes to Pennypacker for a delayed reply caused by a misplaced file.
subfiles.title: Letter of Apology from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Isaac A. Pennypacker for Misplaced File

subfiles.about: Inquires whether American citizens in Japan may convey property by will and asks about Japanese probate, taxes, and treaties.
subfiles.from: John B. Wilson (Secretary of State of Georgia, Atlanta)
subfiles.summary: Georgia's Secretary of State asks Hull about Americans' property and inheritance rights in Japan, and relevant treaties.
subfiles.title: Letter from John B. Wilson (Georgia Secretary of State) on Property and Inheritance Laws in Japan
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull (Secretary of State, Washington, D.C.)

subfiles.about: Internal memorandum analyzing Japanese statutory law and court practice governing the administration of foreign estates and wills.
subfiles.from: E. H. D. (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: Memo: Japanese courts apply a deceased's national law, but provincial courts often decline jurisdiction unless Japan has real property.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Division of Far Eastern Affairs on Estate Settlement Practices in Japan
subfiles.to: Mr. Ward and Mr. Turner (Department of State)

subfiles.about: Provides comprehensive information and legal excerpts on Japanese probate procedure, alien land laws, and treaty tax provisions.
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore (Assistant Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Assistant Secretary of State R. Walton Moore sends a detailed informational reply to the Secretary of State of Georgia answering questions regarding Japanese probate and property law. Quoting published legal digests by J. E. de Becker and Dr. Rokuichiro Masujima, the letter explains that succession and wills of foreigners are governed by their home national and state laws, and succession taxes apply only to property situated in Japan. Moore notes that Article I of the Japanese Alien Land Law of 1925 allows reciprocal restrictions against citizens of countries or states limiting Japanese land rights, but that it has not been invoked against Americans, and cites Article I of the 1894 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation ensuring non-discriminatory taxation.
subfiles.title: Letter from Assistant Secretary R. Walton Moore to John B. Wilson on Japanese Estate and Land Laws
subfiles.to: John B. Wilson (Secretary of State of Georgia, Atlanta)

subfiles.about: Preliminary acknowledgement of Georgia's inquiry on Japanese property rights promising a substantive study and response.
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore (Assistant Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Moore tells Georgia's Secretary State lacks ready data on Japanese property law, promising a fuller reply later.
subfiles.title: Preliminary Acknowledgement from R. Walton Moore to John B. Wilson
subfiles.to: John B. Wilson (Secretary of State of Georgia, Atlanta)

subfiles.about: Identifies American citizens known through diplomatic residence to own land in fee simple in Japan.
subfiles.from: J. W. B. and W. T. T. (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: Memo names four Americans believed to own land in fee simple in Japan, including architect Antonin Raymond.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on American Citizens Owning Land in Fee Simple in Japan

subfiles.about: Inquires whether any treaty permits U.S. citizens to own real estate in Japan to satisfy reciprocity under Idaho's alien land law.
subfiles.from: William H. Witty (Attorney at Law, Pocatello, Idaho)
subfiles.summary: Attorney Witty asks State for any treaty letting a Japanese client own real estate in Idaho under state alien-land law.
subfiles.title: Letter from William H. Witty Inquiring on Treaty Rights for Japanese Land Ownership in Idaho

subfiles.about: Reviews the 1923 Idaho alien land statute and its strict requirement of an authorizing treaty for land tenure by ineligible aliens.
subfiles.summary: Keating advises Idaho's treaty requirement means Japanese domestic reciprocity statutes need not be mentioned in reply.
subfiles.title: Internal Memorandum by J. T. Keating on Idaho Alien Land Statute

subfiles.about: Informs William H. Witty that no treaty in force permits U.S. citizens to own real property in Japan, citing the 1911 treaty.
subfiles.from: Charles M. Barnes (Chief, Treaty Division, for the Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Barnes tells Witty no treaty lets Americans own real estate in Japan, since the 1911 treaty's property clause excludes fee simple ownership.
subfiles.title: Letter from Charles M. Barnes to William H. Witty on Treaty Provisions and Real Estate Ownership

subfiles.about: Inquires by telegram whether the 1911 treaty clause on commercial and residential leasing is in force and whether time limitations exist.
subfiles.summary: Cherry and Hull ask State whether the 1911 treaty's leasing rights remain in force, and any commercial-lease term limits.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Cherry and Hull Inquiring on Treaty Leasing Provisions and Commercial Lease Limits

subfiles.about: Telegraphs Cherry and Hull confirming that Article I of the 1911 treaty is in force and contains no specific term limits on commercial leases.
subfiles.summary: Hull confirms the 1911 treaty's leasing clause remains in force, with no specific limit on commercial lease duration.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Cordell Hull to Cherry and Hull Clarifying Commercial Lease Terms Under 1911 Treaty

subfiles.about: Cross-references a labor protest against the establishment and property acquisition of a Mitsukoshi department store in Honolulu.
subfiles.from: Metal Trades Council of Hawaii (via Department of Labor)
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Hawaii's Metal Trades Council protests Japanese aliens buying Honolulu property to open a Mitsukoshi store.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet on Protest Against Mitsukoshi Department Store in Honolulu
subfiles.to: Department of State / Department of Labor
